This post nails why we why we should take the Riemann Hypothesis breakthrough very seriously, even beyond math. We’re entering an era where solving problems will look very different from how we solved them in the past. “This is not theory-building in the usual sense. It is something much weirder and more alien. The best human mathematicians know how to build theory, painstakingly, to reach a goal. But no human brain, on its own, is capable of creating a wormhole that requires a 25,000 page long tour through existing infrastructure with no obvious or realistic connection to the goal. But huge credit to Levent here: I think no current AI, on its own, is capable of this either.” It used to be the case that to solve a particular problem - code, life sciences, math, cyber, engineering, and so on - you were ultimately bound by how much information an individual or team could retain and understand about the space. More information or more team members don’t always help, because it gets harder to connect the dots or coordinate amongst everyone. AI changes that completely. For the first time ever we can decouple the human context limits and ability to work through information from our ability to drive productivity or discoveries. This is likely not just a small increase in the kinds of discoveries we can drive, but a qualitative shift in human output. Now every single form of prior art, insight, past research, past decision, or unrelated breakthrough, can be used for the discovery or creation of something new. This is useful for anything from cybersecurity to life sciences research. Agents will be able to correlate entirely unrelated work to a separate project; scan every bit of data in your enterprise for solving a problem; and so on. The solutions may not be as elegant as they were in the past, but we sure will have far more of them. We’re only in the first couple of months of actually understanding the implications of this but it’s clearly going to drive a lot of change.
Forget second brain. Third brain.

headline: If you are a product leader, here is a simple exercise: draw out your product lifecycle. e.g. market understanding -> design -> development -> GTM. Chances are your PMs spend more time in some stages than others - because of the nature of your product, your org or their comfort zones. This is a handoff-heavy, lossy process. Now ask yourself: using AI, how much deeper can PMs go on every stage? PMs should be able to - build a much deeper, broader understanding of users and the market - iterate fast from ideas to working prototypes - explore the codebase to study technical constraints and tradeoffs - run their own analytics and investigate questions as they emerge - understand the GTM funnel deeply enough to shape product strategy Now, this is not about PMs replacing every role. As the function that spans the entire lifecycle, this is about raising the bar on the PM role, so they combine their breadth with much greater depth.
